c.st: Ask HN: How do you work as a tech lead?
c.x: I'd highly recommend reading The Manager's Path by Camille Fournier. It has great directional guidance for folks starting in leadership (and experienced ones as well).

c.st: Ask HN: How to move from dev role to management/team lead role?
c.x:
If you have an interest in the managerial career track, talk to you manager. In engineering it’s relatively rare for people who are good developers to be interested in management.

There are two books I highly recommend to anyone considering this move. The Manager’s Path is one. The Making of a Manager is the other.

If you have any concrete questions, I’d be happy to answer them. Contact info is in the profile.

c.st: From engineer to manager: A practical guide to your first months in leadership
c.x: As a related aside, the best practical book on progressing through management ranks as an engineer that I've found is The Manager's Path by Camille Fournier. Highly recommended.

c.st: Ask HN: Which resources would you recommend on software mentorship?
c.x:
I read The Manager's Path and I was not impressed.
She has one chapter on mentoring and the advice is very vague and hard to put into action.

Sources I would recommend:

Peopleware: Productive Projects and Teams Tom DeMarco and Tim Lister

The Mythical Man-Month: Essays on Software Engineering Fred Brooks

Software Craftsmanship: The New Imperative Pete McBreen. Includes several sections on managing and mentoring software developers from apprentice through journeyman to mastery

c.st: Denmark will plant 1B trees and convert 10% of farmland into forest
c.x: Before anyone jumps into this book I would caution against it. This book had many very cool ideas and moments. The way it played out felt very "real". However, in the end there was very little actual story and was very boring at times. I actively dislike Neal Stephenson but if you want a near-future climate story I would recommend Termination Shock over Ministry For The Future. Just a random internet person's two cents.

c.st: Scientists propose glacier geoengineering to avoid sea level rise
c.x:
Keep in mind that we can halt global warming any time we wish with about $5-10b worth of high altitude sulphur injections. That’s a per year price. EdwardTeller, inventor of the hydrogen bomb, introduced this idea. One classic argument against it is “termination shock” — ending the program could be disastrous.

But I tend to think we should be researching the hell out of this topic. We’ve already geoengineered the whole earth already—it’s just that we ought to get good at it.

c.st: Oceans hit highest temperature on record
c.x: 'Termination shock' will be a very real threat, and lets not pretend that injecting sulfides into the atmosphere is going to improve air quality or help the ozone layer.  Best option is to rapidly cut emissions, but I think we can already see that we're not going to chose the best option here.  Hopefully SAI can give us the time we need to decarbonize, but I'm sick that we're gonna have to geoengineer at all.

c.st: Discworld on Page and Screen, Part 1: Serious Comedy
c.x:
…first two Discworld novels are much weaker than later books in the series. Guards Guards is just a much better first book to read, that or Equal Rites is more representative of the quality Discworld would come to have.

Then again my first Discworld novel was Making Money and I loved it even without context (and the “Industrial Revolution” sub-series starting with moving pictures remains my favorite to this day), so you could probably just start at Sourcery and go from there…

c.st: Royal Mail to Issue “Terry Pratchett’s Discworld” Stamps
c.x:
My personal favourite: Equal Rites (I found the balance between humour and message just perfect, and the message is incredibly humane).

The funniest: Pyramids (The groan-inducing punchline about the brothers alone is worth the price of admission, and it's basically stand-alone!)

The best: Night Watch (Sam Vimes' moral anger in full glory).

Weakest: Either Monstruous Regiment or Carpe Jugulum.
